items.readable_text:
Content:
We can apply quantifiers to predicates with more than one variable.

Content:
For example, the statement

Content:
[MATH: \forall m \in \mathbb{N}, \, \exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, n > m]

Content:
reads as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] For all [MATH: m \in \mathbb{N},] there exists [MATH: n \in \mathbb{Z}] such that [MATH: n > m.]

Content:
This statement is true. Informally, it states that given any natural number [MATH: {\color{blue}{m}},] there is an integer [MATH: {\color{red}{n}}] that's larger than [MATH: {\color{blue}{m}}.]

Content:
- If [MATH: {\color{blue}{m}}={\color{blue}{1}}\in \mathbb N] and we select [MATH: {\color{red}{n}}={\color{red}{2}}\in \mathbb Z,] we have [MATH: {\color{red}{2}} > {\color{blue}{1}}] which is true. [MATH: \quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]
- If [MATH: {\color{blue}{m}}={\color{blue}{2}}\in \mathbb N] and we select [MATH: {\color{red}{n}}={\color{red}{3}}\in \mathbb Z,] we have [MATH: {\color{red}{3}} > {\color{blue}{2}}] which is true. [MATH: \quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]
- If [MATH: {\color{blue}{m}}={\color{blue}{3}}\in \mathbb N] and we select [MATH: {\color{red}{n}}={\color{red}{4}}\in \mathbb Z,] we have [MATH: {\color{red}{4}} > {\color{blue}{3}}] which is true. [MATH: \quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

Content:
And so on. It's easy to see that this statement is true since for any [MATH: m\in\mathbb N,] we can simply select [MATH: n = m+1,] and thus [MATH: n > m.]

Content:
Watch out! The order in which the quantifiers are stated is very important. If we swap the quantifiers in this example, we get
[MATH: \exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, \forall m \in \mathbb{N}, \, n > m]
which reads as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] There exists [MATH: n \in \mathbb{Z}] such that for all [MATH: m \in \mathbb{N},] [MATH: n > m.]

Content:
This new statement has an entirely different meaning! Informally, it states that there is an integer [MATH: n] that's larger than every natural number, which is false!

Content:
However, quantifiers of the same type can be swapped. For example,

Content:
[MATH: \exists m \in \mathbb{N}, \, \exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, n > m
\: \equiv \:
\exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, \exists m \in \mathbb{N}, \, n > m.]

Content:
Finally, if we have two or more quantifiers of the same type defined over the same domain, we can write only one quantifier followed by the corresponding variables.

Content:
For example, the (false) statement
[MATH: \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, \, \forall y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x \leq y]
can be written more compactly as
[MATH: \forall \, x,y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x \leq y.]

Content:
Similarly, the (true) statement
[MATH: ∃x ∈ R, ∃y ∈ R, x ≤ y]
can be written as
[MATH: \exists \, x,y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x \leq y.]

Content:
We'll learn more about determining the truth value of a statement containing multiple quantifiers later in the lesson.

Content:
This statement is true. Informally, it states that given any natural number [MATH: {\color{blue}{m}},] there is an integer [MATH: {\color{red}{n}}] that's larger than [MATH: {\color{blue}{m}}.]

Content:
- If [MATH: {\color{blue}{m}}={\color{blue}{1}}\in \mathbb N] and we select [MATH: {\color{red}{n}}={\color{red}{2}}\in \mathbb Z,] we have [MATH: {\color{red}{2}} > {\color{blue}{1}}] which is true. [MATH: \quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]
- If [MATH: {\color{blue}{m}}={\color{blue}{2}}\in \mathbb N] and we select [MATH: {\color{red}{n}}={\color{red}{3}}\in \mathbb Z,] we have [MATH: {\color{red}{3}} > {\color{blue}{2}}] which is true. [MATH: \quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}]

And so on. It's easy to see that this statement is true since for any [MATH: m\in\mathbb N,] we can simply select [MATH: n = m+1,] and thus [MATH: n > m.]

Content:
Watch out! The order in which the quantifiers are stated is very important. If we swap the quantifiers in this example, we get
[MATH: \exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, \forall m \in \mathbb{N}, \, n > m]
which reads as follows:

Content:

Content:
This new statement has an entirely different meaning! Informally, it states that there is an integer [MATH: n] that's larger than every natural number, which is false!

Content:
However, quantifiers of the same type can be swapped. For example,

Content:
[MATH: \exists m \in \mathbb{N}, \, \exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, n > m
\: \equiv \:
\exists n \in \mathbb{Z}, \, \exists m \in \mathbb{N}, \, n > m.]

Finally, if we have two or more quantifiers of the same type defined over the same domain, we can write only one quantifier followed by the corresponding variables.

Content:
For example, the (false) statement

can be written more compactly as
[MATH: \forall \, x,y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x \leq y.]

Similarly, the (true) statement

Item 6 — Tutorial: Free and Bound Occurrences of Variables

Content:
The occurrence of a variable is called bound if it is placed right next to a quantifier or lies within the scope of a quantifier that uses the same variable. Otherwise, the occurrence is called free.

Content:
For example, let's examine the occurrences of variables in the following statement:

Content:
[MATH: \exists y \in \mathbb{N} \big( \, x > 0 \Rightarrow \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, y < 10 \, \big).]

Content:
- The following occurrence of [MATH: y] is bound since it is placed right next to the quantifier [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\exists}{:}]
[MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\exists} \!\! \underset{\substack{\phantom{.} \[4pt] \uparrow \[6pt] \large\phantom{.}\bbox[2pt,Moccasin]{\text{b}}}}{y} \!\! \in \mathbb{N} \big( \, x > 0 \Rightarrow \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, y < 10 \, \big)]
- The following occurrence of [MATH: x] is free since it isn't placed right next to a quantifier and it doesn't lie within the scope of a quantifier that uses [MATH: x{:}]
[MATH: \exists y \in \mathbb{N} \big( \, \underset{\substack{\phantom{.} \[4pt] \uparrow \[6pt] \large\phantom{.}\bbox[2pt,LightBlue]{\text{f}}}}{x} \!\! > 0 \Rightarrow \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, y < 10 \, \big)]
- The following occurrence of [MATH: x] is bound since it is placed right next to the quantifier [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\forall}{:}]
[MATH: \exists y \in \mathbb{N} \big( \, x > 0 \Rightarrow \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\forall} \!\! \underset{\substack{\phantom{.} \[4pt] \uparrow \[6pt] \large\phantom{.}\bbox[2pt,Moccasin]{\text{b}}}}{x} \!\! \in \mathbb{R}, y < 10 \, \big)]
- The following occurrence of [MATH: y] is bound since it lies within the scope of the quantifier [MATH: \exists y] that uses [MATH: y{:}]
[MATH: ∃y]

Content:
So, in our expression, we have:

Content:
- two occurrences of [MATH: y,] both of which are bound, and
- two occurrences of [MATH: x,] where one is free, and another is bound.

Content:
[MATH: \exists \bbox[2pt,Moccasin]{y} \in \mathbb{N} \big( \, \bbox[2pt,LightBlue]{x} > 0 \Rightarrow \big( \, \forall \bbox[2pt,Moccasin]{x} \in \mathbb{R}, \bbox[2pt,Moccasin]{y} < 10 \, \big) \, \big)]

Content:
Distinguishing between free and bound occurrences is important since we are allowed to substitute values into free occurrences of variables. In particular, since the first occurrence of [MATH: \bbox[2pt,LightBlue]{x}] is free, we can substitute concrete values for this variable (but not for the other occurrence of [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Moccasin]{x}]).

Content:
Therefore, the above expression can be viewed as a predicate of one variable ([MATH: \bbox[2pt,LightBlue]{x}]) since all occurrences of [MATH: y] are bound.

Item 10 — Tutorial: The Truth Value of a Statement Involving Nested Quantifiers

Content:
Consider the statement

Content:
[MATH: \forall\, m \in \mathbb{N}, \, \forall\, n \in \mathbb{N}, \, m > n]

Content:
that reads as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] For all natural [MATH: m] and [MATH: n,] we have [MATH: m > n.]

Content:
Is the statement true or false? To figure this out, we proceed as described below.

Content:
First, let's write down the inner predicate and determine its truth set:
[MATH: P(m): \quad \forall\, n \in \mathbb{N}, \, m > n.]
Notice that this is a predicate in the variable [MATH: m] since [MATH: m] is a free variable in the [MATH: P(m)] statement.

Content:
The predicate [MATH: P(m)] is false for all values [MATH: m \in \mathbb {N}.] For example,
[MATH: P(1) : \quad \forall\, n \in \mathbb{N}, \, 1 > n]
is false since we can take [MATH: n=1.] Similarly,
[MATH: P(2): \quad \forall\, n \in \mathbb{N}, \, 2 > n]
is false, since we can take [MATH: n=2.] In general, it's sufficient to take [MATH: n=m] for any value of [MATH: m.] As a result, the truth set of [MATH: P(m)] is [MATH: T_P=\emptyset.]

Content:
Now, notice that we can write our original statement as follows:
[MATH: \forall\, m \in \mathbb{N}, \, \forall\, n \in \mathbb{N}, \, m > n \: \equiv \: \forall m \in \mathbb{N}, \, P(m).]
This statement is true whenever the inner predicate [MATH: P(m)] is true over the universal set [MATH: \mathbb N.] However, this is not the case, as we discovered above.

Content:
Therefore, the statement [MATH: \forall\, m \in \mathbb{N}, \, \forall\, n \in \mathbb{N}, \, m > n] is false.

Item 11 — Example: Finding the Truth Value of a Statement Involving Nested Quantifiers

Example Prompt:
Which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: \exists \, y \in \mathbb{R}, \, 2+y=0.]
2. The truth set of the predicate [MATH: \big( \, \exists y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x+y = 0 \, \big)] is [MATH: \mathbb{R}.]
3. [MATH: \forall\, x \in \mathbb{R}, \, \exists y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x+y=0.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, notice that the statement

[MATH: \forall\, x \in \mathbb{R}, \, \exists y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x+y=0]

from option III reads as follows:

[MATH: \qquad] For every real [MATH: x] there exists real [MATH: y] such that [MATH: x+y=0.]

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true since [MATH: 2+y=0] for some real number [MATH: y] (e.g., for [MATH: y=-2]).
- Statement II is true. The predicate
[MATH: P(x): \quad \exists \, y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x+y=0]
is true for any real [MATH: x.] For example,
[MATH: P(1): \quad \exists \, y \in \mathbb{R}, \, 1 + y=0]
is true since we can take [MATH: y=-1.] Similarly,
[MATH: P(2): \quad \exists \, y \in \mathbb{R}, \, 2+ y=0]
is true since we can take [MATH: y=-2.] And so on. In general, it's sufficient to take [MATH: y=-x.]
- Statement III is true. The sentence
[MATH: \big( \, \forall\, x \in \mathbb{R}, \, \exists y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x+y=0 \, \big)]
can be written as
[MATH: \forall\, x \in \mathbb{R} \, \big( \, \underbrace{\exists y \in \mathbb{R}, \, x+y=0}_{P(x)} \, \big)]
which is true whenever the inner predicate [MATH: P(x)] is true over the universal set [MATH: \mathbb R.] And, according to statement II, this is the case.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."
